title: The Chorus
author: Alexandre Dias
excerpt: It started with the E above high C. Élise Marchant was warming up alone in the small practice room at the top of a narrow staircase, and she heard, quite clearly, a second note. It was not an overtone. It was another note. And it had come out of her own throat.

chapters.title: The Second Note
chapters.body:
It started with the E above high C.

Élise Marchant was thirty-one years old, and she had been, for eleven years, a working soprano — not a famous one, not one of the sopranos whose faces appeared on posters at the Palais Garnier, but a good one, a reliable one, the sort of singer who was engaged for choral work at Notre-Dame and for occasional oratorio at smaller festivals in the Loire, and who taught, three afternoons a week, at a small conservatoire in the tenth arrondissement.

She was warming up.

She was in the small practice room she had rented for years at the back of the conservatoire, at the top of a narrow staircase that no one ever climbed unless they meant to, and she was going through her scales, and she had reached the E above high C in the arpeggio she had been singing since she was seventeen, when she heard, quite clearly, a second note.

It was not an overtone. She knew overtones. Overtones were the natural harmonic ghosts that hung above a sung note, and every good soprano had learned to hear them and to shape her voice around them. This was not an overtone. This was another note. A definite note. A note that was not part of the E she was singing, and that had, so far as she could tell, come out of her own throat at the same moment.

She stopped.

The room was silent. The single window looked out onto a small grey courtyard. The old upright piano, whose C above middle C she had struck to give herself the reference, sat in the corner and offered nothing.

She struck the E again on the piano. She sang the E. She held it, quietly, listening.

There was only the E.

She let the note fall. She stood in the practice room and breathed for a moment. She had, she told herself, imagined it. She was tired. She had been at Notre-Dame the previous evening for a rehearsal of a Fauré Requiem that had run past ten, and she had walked home in the cold, and had slept badly, and had eaten only an apple for breakfast. Tired sopranos misheard themselves all the time. It was a well-documented phenomenon. She was, she told herself, being ridiculous.

She struck the E again.

She sang.

The second note was there again.

It was not exactly an interval away from the E. Élise had perfect pitch, and had had it since childhood, and could name any note that was named in her presence within a semitone of when it was struck. The second note was not any note she could name. It was slightly flat of an F sharp — perhaps a quarter tone below, perhaps a third of a tone. It was a note that did not exist in the twelve-tone system in which she had been trained. It sat outside the scale, in a small space between the notes that were supposed to be there, and it hummed there quietly, alongside her E, patient.

She stopped again.

She sat down on the piano bench.

She looked at the small grey courtyard outside the window. She looked at her hands in her lap. She looked at the piano.

She said, very quietly, in the empty room: *what was that.*

She was not asking the room.

—

She finished the scales.

She had considered, sitting on the piano bench, that she might not finish. She had considered leaving. She had considered walking down the stairs and going home to her small flat in the eleventh, and sitting there, and not thinking about any of this until she had had time to sleep properly. But she had also considered — and this consideration had, in the end, won — that if she left now without knowing whether the second note would come again, she would spend the rest of the day and the whole of the night listening for it in her mind, and she would sleep no better than she had.

She had, she thought, better find out.

She had run the scales again. Slowly. Note by note. The second note did not appear on the C. It did not appear on the C sharp. It did not appear on the D or the D sharp or the E flat. It appeared on the E — as it had before — sitting a quarter tone below F sharp, patient, warm.

It appeared on the F.

On the F it was a different note. It was slightly sharp of A, this time, hanging above her F, again at some interval outside the scale.

On the F sharp it was gone.

On the G it was back. On the G it sat slightly above B flat.

She kept going. Note by note. The second note came and went. It did not follow any pattern of intervals she could immediately name. It did not appear in unison with her sung note, and it did not appear a third above, or a fifth above, or an octave above. It appeared, when it appeared, at intervals that were slightly off from every interval she had ever been taught, in a scale that was not any scale she knew.

By the time she had reached the top of her range, she had catalogued the second note on eleven pitches out of the seventeen she had tried.

She stopped.

She sat on the piano bench.

She noted, with a strange precision, that she was not exactly frightened. She was — she checked — surprised. She was very surprised. But underneath the surprise there was something else, some quieter thing that had been sitting under the surprise for the last twenty minutes, and had been waiting for her to notice it.

The quiet thing was: *this is the sound I have been waiting to hear.*

She did not know what she meant.

She had never, that she knew of, been waiting for any particular sound. She had spent her life making sounds. She had sung all of her life. She had, at four, been the child who sang in the small kitchen while her mother made bread. At seven, she had been the one chosen for the small solo at Christmas. At twelve she had begun serious training. At eighteen she had won a small competition and had, on the strength of it, gone to the conservatoire. She had made her career.

She had made her career, mostly, by understanding one thing: that her voice was pretty and reliable and technically clean, and that this had been enough to get her work but had not been enough to get her the work she wanted. She had heard, since she was young, the voices of the great sopranos — the Callas voice, the Norman voice, the little-known voice of a Bulgarian mezzo she had once heard on a recording who had made her weep for reasons she could not name — and she had understood, quietly, that her own voice would not do that. It was not going to be that voice. It was going to be the voice it was.

She had made her peace with this.

She had made her peace with it, and had done good work, and had been paid, and had made a small good life, and had not, in all the making of the peace, ever entirely lost the small internal listening for the other voice. The voice she was not. The voice she would have wanted to have.

She sat on the piano bench in the small practice room at the top of the narrow staircase, and she understood, with a coldness that came from below her thinking, that the second note was that voice.

—

She stood up. She went to the window. She looked at the small grey courtyard.

She thought: *this is not possible.*

She thought: *I have imagined this.*

She thought: *I have been thinking about the other voice for so long that I have begun to hear it in my own singing, and there is a name for what that is, and the name is a diagnosis.*

She looked at her hands on the windowsill.

She thought: *no.*

She thought this last thing with the calm certainty she had felt once or twice in her life, at moments when something was true whether or not she preferred it to be. She thought it, and she knew it was true, and she did not feel any impulse to argue with it. The second note had not been a mishearing. She was a soprano. She had heard hundreds of thousands of notes in her life, from her own throat and from the throats of others, and she knew the difference between a note that was there and a note that she was inventing. The second note had been there.

Something in her had made a second note.

Not something *in* her, exactly. Something *of* her. Some part of her voice, working in a way it had not worked yesterday, had produced a note her voice had never produced. And the note had come from a place her voice did not, so far as she had known before, contain.

She turned from the window.

She walked back to the piano.

She sat down. She struck the E above high C. She sang the E.

The second note came in, quiet and warm, a quarter tone below F sharp.

She listened.

She listened for a long time — she held the note as long as she could hold it, and then she took a breath and sang it again, and she listened. The second note held with her. The second note was there whenever she sang the E, and it was gone whenever she stopped singing. She could not, when she tried, sing the second note by itself. She sang F sharp; only F sharp came. She sang the E, and the second note appeared with the E, faithful.

She sang the E, and she closed her eyes.

The second note was — she was not sure of this word, but no other word was available — the second note was *listening.*

She did not know how she knew.

She knew.

She stopped singing.

The second note fell silent with her voice.

She sat on the piano bench for a long time.

At last she stood up. She closed the piano lid. She took her coat from the hook. She turned out the lamp on the piano.

She walked down the narrow staircase, and she went home, and she did not sing again that day.

—

She dreamed, that night, that she was a child standing in her mother's kitchen. She was, in the dream, perhaps five. Her mother was at the counter making bread. The kitchen was full of the smell of yeast and of the soap her mother had used on the tiles, and Élise was singing, quietly, to herself, some small tuneless song she had made up.

She was singing in two voices.

She was singing, in the dream, in her own child voice, and in another voice — a voice deeper and older, a voice she did not, in the dream, recognize as anyone's, that ran alongside her own like a second river beside a first.

In the dream her mother had turned around.

Her mother had looked at her.

Her mother had said, in the dream, in the specific tone of the woman her mother had been at that age: *Élise. Stop that.*

And Élise, in the dream, had stopped.

The second voice had faded. She had been left in the small kitchen singing alone, in her one child voice, and her mother had turned back to the bread.

She had, in the dream, understood what she was being told to stop.

She had, in the dream, put the second voice down. She had folded it. She had put it in the small drawer at the back of her own throat where she kept things that her mother did not like. She had understood, in the way children understood things they were not told, that the second voice was not something you were allowed to have, and that if you had it, you kept it quiet, or you got rid of it, and if you did not get rid of it, you at least did not let anyone hear.

She had woken in her small flat in the eleventh, in the dark, at three-thirty in the morning.

She had lain in bed and listened to her own breathing.

She had thought, with the clear cold thinking that came at three-thirty in the morning: *it has been in me since I was five.*

She had thought: *I forgot to keep it hidden this afternoon.*

She had thought, and this thought had brought her, at last, into full waking: *I do not want to hide it anymore.*

chapters.title: Two Voices
chapters.body:
She sang in two voices for the whole of the next week.

She did it in secret. She did it in the small practice room at the top of the narrow staircase, where no one came unless they meant to, with the door locked and the window closed, and she did it as an experiment — carefully, methodically, in the way she had once, at nineteen, systematically worked out the exact conditions under which her upper range would open up. She was a soprano. She had spent her life learning what her voice could do. She was going to learn what her voice could now do that it could not do before, and she was going to do it, at first, in a room where no one would hear.

She found out several things.

The first was that the second voice was not, as she had thought at first, purely reactive. It did not come only when she sang, in the way an overtone came only when the fundamental was there. It came when she sang, yes — but by the third day she had discovered that if she sat very still, and did not sing, and simply *listened*, the second voice could be coaxed. She could feel it, at those moments, as a kind of warm quiet presence in the small hollow at the base of her throat. She could feel it waiting. If she then began to hum, very softly, on a single note, the second voice would rise with her humming — and then, if she stopped humming but kept the small tension in her throat, the second voice would sometimes go on, alone, for a second or two, before it faded.

It was capable of independent action.

This was the first thing.

The second thing was that the second voice had — she had no other word — a *temperament.* It preferred certain vowels. It was strongest on the open A. It was weakest on the closed U, which almost silenced it. It preferred the middle of her range to the top. It preferred slow notes to fast ones. If she sang a rapid coloratura passage, the second voice fell away almost entirely, unable to keep up; if she held a long slow note, the second voice grew louder and more definite over the length of the holding, as if it were, given time, filling itself out.

She had thought about this. She had thought about a long-held note as a kind of *space* that the second voice could enter, and about the coloratura as a kind of terrain across which the second voice could not travel. She had wondered, in her notebook — she had begun to keep a notebook, in the way she had kept a notebook once at eighteen for her first serious voice teacher — whether the second voice was, in a strange way, *slower* than she was. Slower to move. Slower to place itself in a note. Slower to leave.

She had written: *it is older than I am.*

She had underlined it.

The third thing she had learned — and this was the thing that had made her stop the experiments, for two days, and had made her afraid — was that the second voice was becoming louder.

On the first day it had been, at its clearest, perhaps a quarter of the volume of her sung note. It had been a whisper alongside a speaking voice. By the fourth day, when she sang the long A on the E she had first heard it on, the second voice was perhaps half the volume of her voice. By the sixth day it was three-quarters.

By the seventh day it was, when she sang, as loud as she was.

She had stopped, on the seventh day, in the middle of a long held note, because she had realized suddenly that the two voices coming out of her — hers and the second — were, at that moment, equally present, and that anyone standing outside the door of the practice room would have heard two women singing.

She had stood in the room.

She had put her hand at her throat.

She had said, aloud, in her own single speaking voice: *stop.*

The second voice had, obediently, gone silent.

She had sat down on the piano bench.

She had understood, sitting on the piano bench, that whatever was happening to her was no longer a curiosity. It had been a curiosity for a week. It was, now, something more. It was becoming a *fact* of her — a second capacity she was going to have to decide, actively, whether to permit or to hide.

And she had understood, with the calm cold thinking of the morning of the eighth day, that she was not going to hide it. She had spent twenty-six years hiding it. She had put it in the small drawer at the back of her throat at five, when her mother had told her to stop, and she had kept it there. It had, this week, gotten out. She was not going to put it back.

—

She had a rehearsal that Thursday.

It was for a small performance of Vivaldi's Gloria at a church in the Marais, arranged by an old colleague from the conservatoire who ran a small choral society, and she was to sing the soprano solo in the second movement. She had done the piece before. She knew it. It was, ordinarily, an easy engagement.

She had gone to the rehearsal in the afternoon.

The church was cold. The choir was already assembled when she arrived — perhaps thirty singers, a mixture of professionals and skilled amateurs, most of them known to her from other engagements. The conductor was a small precise man named Bernard whom she had known for years. He had waved her forward, cheerfully, when she came in.

They had begun.

She had sung the first movement in the chorus, as second soprano, and had been careful. She had held the second voice quiet at the back of her throat, the way she had held it for twenty-six years, and she had produced the small clean line she always produced, and no one had heard anything different.

The second movement had come.

She had walked forward. She had taken her place beside the conductor. She had waited for the ritornello to end. She had opened her mouth.

She had begun, in her single voice, to sing the opening phrase of the *Et in terra pax.*

The second voice had come in on the third bar.

She had, at first, tried to hold it down. She had felt it rise at the back of her throat, and she had, with the twenty-six-year-old reflex of a child in her mother's kitchen, tried to press it back. She had done this in the way a professional soprano does anything mid-performance, without visible effort, with the small internal muscles of her breath, and she had, for perhaps two bars, succeeded.

Then, on a long held A, she had — and she remembered this afterwards clearly — she had *decided* to let it come.

She had made the decision in a fraction of a second, standing in the cold church at four in the afternoon, in front of thirty singers and a conductor she had known for twenty years, and she had known when she made it that it was the decision of her life.

She had let the second voice come.

It had come.

It had risen alongside her sung line, quietly at first, and then, as she held the long A, more definitely — a full second voice, singing a note that was not the note she was singing, a note that sat outside the scale of the piece, a note that had not been written by Vivaldi. It had held with her for perhaps four seconds. She had, from where she stood, been able to feel it filling the small space of the church. She had, from where she stood, been able to see Bernard's baton falter.

She had finished the phrase.

She had closed her mouth.

There had been a silence.

Bernard had stood at his podium with his baton still raised. The choir had stood behind him without moving. Somewhere in the middle of the church, a woman had begun to weep, quietly, into her hand.

Bernard had said, at last, in the small careful voice of a man who did not know what he was saying:

*Élise. What was that.*

She had said: *my voice.*

Bernard had said: *both of them?*

She had said: *both of them.*

Bernard had put down his baton. He had come down from the podium. He had walked to where she stood, and he had looked at her for a long moment.

He had said: *may we go on?*

She had said: *if you would like.*

He had said: *I would like.*

He had gone back to the podium.

They had gone on.

She had sung, for the rest of the rehearsal, in two voices. Bernard had not stopped her. The choir had sung around her. The woman weeping in the middle of the church had gone on weeping, softly, until she had left, at the end of the rehearsal, without looking at anyone.

When it was over Bernard had come to her again.

He had said: *I do not know what that is.*

She had said: *neither do I.*

He had said: *I would like you to sing on Saturday.*

She had said: *I would like to sing on Saturday.*

He had nodded. He had turned away. He had begun to gather his score.

He had said, without looking at her, in the small still voice of a man who had heard something he was not going to be able to describe to his wife when he got home:

*I thought, when I heard it — I thought there were two of you.*

She had said, quietly, so only he could hear:

*There are.*

—

She had walked home through the Marais in the early evening. The streets had been busy. She had walked without hurry, and she had felt, in her chest and in her throat and in the small hollow at the base of her neck, the presence of the second voice, quiet now, resting, no longer hidden.

She had thought: *I have been carrying you for twenty-six years.*

She had thought: *I am tired of carrying you alone.*

She had thought, and this thought had come with a warmth she had not felt since she was a child in a small kitchen: *you can come out now. It is safe.*

At the corner of the Rue des Rosiers she had hummed, softly, a single note.

The second voice had come with her, quiet and warm, and had held with her for the length of the note, and had faded when she had stopped humming.

She had walked on.

She had not, in her whole life, ever felt less alone.

chapters.title: The Chorus
chapters.body:
The Vivaldi was on a Saturday evening.

She spent Friday preparing. She rested her voice. She drank tea with lemon. She ate lightly. She slept, in the afternoon, for two hours, because she had learned that a nap on the day before a performance was worth more to her than any amount of vocal exercise. She went for a walk in the small park near her flat at dusk, and she thought, quietly, about what she was going to do.

She had thought about it all week.

She had thought about it as she had walked home from the rehearsal in the Marais, and she had thought about it as she had lain in bed that night unable to sleep, and she had thought about it on the days between then and now. She had thought about it while she had done small ordinary things — her marketing, her laundry, the writing of a letter to her mother that had been overdue for three weeks — and she had thought about it in the way one thought about the important things, at the back of every other thought, in the quiet ongoing under-thought that ran under the surface of a life.

She had thought about it, and she had made her decision.

She was going to sing the *Et in terra pax* the way she had sung it at the rehearsal.

She was going to sing it in two voices. She was going to sing it in front of the fifty or so people who had bought tickets to a small choral performance in a small church in the Marais on a Saturday evening in November, and she was going to sing it fully — with the second voice not hidden, not muffled, not pressed back into the small drawer at the back of her throat, but fully released, fully present, fully hers.

She had, she thought, spent enough of her life keeping the drawer closed.

She was thirty-one. She had, if the ordinary luck held, another forty or fifty years of singing ahead of her. She could spend those forty or fifty years the way she had spent the last twenty-six, in the practiced narrowing of what she was into what other people could bear to hear. Or she could spend them differently. She could sing with what she had. She could sing with the whole of what she had.

She had made her choice on Wednesday afternoon, and she had not, since Wednesday afternoon, been afraid.

—

She arrived at the church at six.

The performance was at seven. She had time to warm up in the small vestry behind the altar, and she did so quietly, and thoroughly, and without letting the second voice come. She was saving it. She wanted it fresh.

She had, before she left the flat, put on the black dress she wore for performances, and had done her hair, and had put on her small silver earrings. She looked, when she looked in the mirror above the sink in the vestry, like a woman who was about to sing at a church concert in November. She looked composed. She looked like every other soprano who had come to this church, or any church, to earn a small quiet fee at a Saturday-evening performance.

She looked at herself for a long moment.

She thought: *I am going to be, in an hour, the first person in my life to hear what I actually sound like.*

The thought was strange. It sat in her mind as a strange sentence. She had heard herself sing every day for twenty-six years. She had listened to recordings of her own voice for hundreds of hours. She had refined and shaped and disciplined her voice for her whole professional life. And she was going to hear, in an hour, what she actually sounded like, for the first time.

She would not, she understood, be the only one.

Bernard would hear. The choir would hear. The audience of fifty would hear. Somewhere in the church would be, perhaps, another woman who had, at five, been told by her own mother to stop singing in the second voice. Somewhere in the church would be another child. Somewhere in the church would be the small other listener she had felt in every audience she had ever sung to and had never, so far as she knew, been able to reach.

She was going to reach that listener now.

She combed her hair once more.

She went into the church.

—

The church was full.

She had not expected this. There had been perhaps fifty tickets sold, but the pews were full, and there were people standing at the back, and the small aisle along the north wall had, when she came in, several extra chairs pulled into it. Word had, apparently, spread. Someone from the rehearsal — she never knew who — had told someone, and that someone had told two others, and by seven o'clock on Saturday there were, she estimated, perhaps a hundred and twenty people in the church, on a cold November evening, come to hear the small Vivaldi at Notre-Dame-des-Blancs-Manteaux.

Bernard did not look surprised.

He was, when she took her seat in the choir, calm. He nodded to her. He raised his baton. He gave the small brisk downbeat that had begun their rehearsals since they were both young.

The choir began.

She sang the first movement in the second soprano line, as at the rehearsal, holding the second voice quiet. She sang cleanly and well. She was not, at that moment, herself. She was the trained instrument she had been for eleven years. She was doing her job.

The second movement came.

She stood. She walked forward. She took her place beside Bernard. She waited for the ritornello.

She looked at the audience.

She saw, in the second pew, a woman weeping already, before the movement had begun. She saw, at the back, a man she did not know, in a grey coat, watching her with an expression she could not read. She saw, at the very back, a young girl of perhaps ten, sitting with her mother, looking at Élise with the specific attention of a child who was, whether or not she knew it, taking notes about the woman she was going to become.

Élise looked at the girl.

The ritornello ended.

She opened her mouth.

She sang the opening phrase of the *Et in terra pax*, and the second voice came in on the second bar, and this time she did not press it back, not even for a moment — she let it come from the beginning, let it fill her throat, let it stand beside her sung line the way it wanted to stand, and she sang the whole of the *Et in terra pax* in two voices.

The church went very quiet.

Not the ordinary quiet of an audience listening. A different quiet. The quiet of a room in which something that had not been heard before was being heard for the first time. The quiet of animals when a predator was near, though there was no predator. The quiet of a small stone dropped into still water, and the way the water was still for a moment before the ripple.

She sang.

She sang the phrase. She sang the melisma. She sang the long held A. She heard, alongside her voice, the second voice — no longer her second voice, no longer secret, no longer folded, but her *other* voice, her chorus, the voice that had been in her since she was five, singing at last the way it had always wanted to sing, in front of a hundred and twenty people who could hear it.

She held the long A.

She held it for six full seconds, longer than she had ever held a note, and the second voice held with her, and the two voices together filled the small church all the way up to the vaulted ceiling and down into every stone corner.

She let the note fall.

There was silence.

The silence held. For four seconds. Five. Six. It was the silence one heard, sometimes, after certain kinds of performance — the silence of an audience that had been changed and was, for a moment, unable to remember what audiences did after music. She had heard it, once, at eighteen, at a concert of a Bulgarian mezzo she had never forgotten.

Then someone at the back began to applaud.

The applause came slowly at first, and then more, and then all of them — the hundred and twenty people in the cold church in the Marais on a Saturday evening in November — were on their feet, applauding for a small soprano nobody had heard of who had, that evening, done something none of them could name.

She stood at the front of the choir.

She let them applaud.

She looked, once, at the girl of ten at the back.

The girl was crying. The mother was holding her, and the girl was crying, and Élise understood, in the small clear thinking of the moment, that the girl was crying because she had recognized something in the two voices — some small thing she had, herself, at ten, folded and put away, and was now beginning to remember she had put away.

Élise nodded to the girl.

The girl, still crying, nodded back.

Élise turned to Bernard.

Bernard raised his baton.

They went on with the Gloria.

—

She did not stop, after that Saturday.

She sang, from then on, in two voices, always. She sang in two voices at every rehearsal, at every performance, at every small church concert she was engaged for, and after some months, at the larger engagements that had begun to come. Word had gotten out. There was a recording, made illegally by someone in the audience at the second performance, that had circulated on a small classical music forum and then had traveled further, and by the following spring Élise Marchant, the small soprano who had made a small quiet career for eleven years, was being written about in the music press, and being invited to festivals she had never dreamed of being invited to, and being asked, by conductors she had admired since her teens, whether she would sing.

She sang.

She sang for the next twenty years. She sang at Salzburg. She sang at La Scala. She sang, at forty-two, at the Palais Garnier, in a program of Mahler that was recorded and won a prize. She sang, in her fifties, less often but with more focus, and taught. She taught, in the small conservatoire in the tenth arrondissement where she had first heard the second voice, a small class of young singers whom she had chosen carefully, and to whom she taught many things, but taught, above all, one thing:

She taught them to listen for the second voice.

She taught them that everyone had one. She taught them that it had, in most cases, been folded very small at some point in early childhood, and put away in the small drawer at the back of the throat where things one was told to stop went, and that it was still there. She taught them how to sit very still, and how to feel it, and how to coax it, and how to let it come.

Some of them found their second voice.

Some of them did not. Some of them, having found it, could not bear it, and put it back. This was permitted. She did not tell them what to do with their second voice. She only told them, and this she told them at every first lesson, that they had one, and that they were allowed to know it was there.

She had one student, a young Korean soprano named Ji-eun who had come to her at nineteen, who had, on the fourth lesson, produced her second voice, and had wept quietly in the practice room afterwards, and had asked Élise:

*How did you know it was there?*

Élise had said: *I had one.*

Ji-eun had said: *and if I had not found it?*

Élise had said: *you would have gone on singing without it. Many people do. It is not a disaster. It is only —* she had paused, choosing the word — *lonelier.*

Ji-eun had nodded.

They had gone on with the lesson.

Élise had died, in the end, at seventy-eight, of the ordinary kind of death that came to sopranos who had been careful with their voices — a small quiet stroke in her sleep, in her small flat in the eleventh, on a Sunday morning in June, with the window open and the sound of the market on the Rue Saint-Antoine drifting in.

Her students had gone on singing. Some of them, the ones who had found their second voices, sang in two voices still, for the rest of their lives. One of them, Ji-eun, had gone on to become a very great soprano indeed, greater than Élise had ever been, and had, in interviews, always attributed the essential thing about her voice to a lesson she had once had, at nineteen, in a small practice room at the top of a narrow staircase in Paris, with a teacher who had told her that there was a second voice in her, and that she was allowed to know it was there.

The recording of the *Et in terra pax* from that first Saturday still exists. It is not, technically, a very good recording. It was made on a small handheld device from the back of a cold church, and there is a great deal of background noise, and the balance is uneven. But it is possible to hear, if one listens carefully, the moment when the second voice comes in.

It comes in on the second bar.

It comes in quiet, and warm, and slightly flat of an F sharp, in a space between the notes that are supposed to be there.

It comes in, and it stays.
